summary: High accuracy is not the same as fair outcomes, and confusing the two is one of the costliest mistakes in AI. Picture this. A company pilots an AI system that screens job applicants and recommends who should advance to the next round. The team runs tests and sees an overall prediction accuracy of 89%. Everyone is pleased. Then someone slices the results by demographic group. The rate at which the system recommends applicants differs by more than 20% across groups. The model is “accurate,” so what went wrong? Accuracy answers a different question Accuracy measures how often a model’s predictions match the labels it was trained on. It doesn’t ask whether those labels were fair to begin with. Suppose the training data is a decade of historical hiring decisions. If those decisions systematically favored some groups, a model that learns them well will score high on accuracy precisely because it has learned to imitate the bias. This is the most likely explanation for the 20% gap. The model learned patterns from biased training data and reproduced them. As the SageMaker documentation explains, models trained on data that reflects existing disparities can reproduce those disparities or even exacerbate them. What it is not A few tempting explanations don’t hold up: “ It’s just statistical noise from different sample sizes. ” Sample-size noise is random and usually small. A consistent gap of 20%+ across groups is a material disparity that demands investigation, not a rounding error. “
title: An 89% Accurate Hiring AI Can Still Be Unfair. Here’s Why.

summary: The MySQL primary was still running. Applications could reach the database. Yet some write requests were taking too long and timing out. The problem wasn't a missing primary. Both replicas had stopped replicating, and semi-synchronous replication had become part of the availability problem. In Part 1 , I covered deploying MySQL with MOCO. Part 2 covered backups, MinIO, and a davfs2 failure. This time, let's look at the replication behavior that matters when things go wrong. The three-instance cluster MOCO uses GTID-based semi-synchronous replication for its normal three-instance MySQL clusters: one writable primary and two read-only replicas. Application | v eks-db-1 PRIMARY | binary log events / \ v v eks-db-0 eks-db-2 REPLICA REPLICA \ / replication ACK With asynchronous replication, the primary can acknowledge a committed transaction to the application without waiting for any replica to confirm receipt. With semi-synchronous replication, the primary waits for the configured number of replicas to acknowledge receiving the transaction's binary-log events . An ACK does not mean the replica has already applied the transaction. With MOCO's normal three-instance configuration, one replica acknowledgement is required. Losing one replica does not necessarily stop writes; the other can still acknowledge them. Losing both removes that acknowledgement path. The configuration that changes everything On the primary, these commands reveal the relevant settings: SHOW GLOBAL VARIABLES LIK

summary: 1. Tokenization Definition: Tokenization is the process of breaking down text into smaller units, called tokens, which can be words, subwords, or even individual characters. These tokens serve as the building blocks that AI models use to process and generate language. How It Works: A sentence like "Artificial Intelligence is powerful." The model tokenizes it into smaller units: Word-level tokenization: ["Artificial", "Intelligence", "is", "powerful", "."] Subword tokenization (e.g., Byte-Pair Encoding): ["Artifi", "cial", "Intelli", "gence", "is", "power", "ful", "."] Character-level tokenization: ["A", "r", "t", "i", "f", "i", "c", "i", "a", "l", ...] Why It Matters: Helps models understand and generate text efficiently. Handles out-of-vocabulary words by breaking them into subwords. Reduces complexity compared to processing raw text. 2. Context Window Definition: The context window refers to the maximum number of tokens an AI model can process at once when generating responses. It determines how much prior text the model "remembers" during inference. How It Works: If a model has a context window of 4,096 tokens, it can only consider the last 4,096 tokens when generating a response. Older parts of a conversation or document may be forgotten unless explicitly included in the prompt. Why It Matters: Short context windows (e.g., 512 tokens) limit long-form coherence. summary: In Understanding Observability with OpenTelemetry and Coffee , I introduced the fundamentals of observability. In Native OpenTelemetry , I explored how OpenTelemetry generates and processes telemetry, how the OpenTelemetry Collector manages telemetry pipelines, and why understanding those pipelines matters when troubleshooting production issues. This article explores the open-source observability ecosystem, from the responsibilities of individual tools to the engineering decisions involved in running them together. OpenTelemetry isn't your observability backend OpenTelemetry is an open-source, vendor-neutral observability framework. Think of OpenTelemetry as the system that standardizes how information leaves each part of the coffee shop. The observability tools help you examine that information and understand what happened.

Operating systems and browsers keep a store of trusted root Certificate Authorities (CAs), such as the roots behind Let's Encrypt or DigiCert. If the site's certificate chains back to one of those roots, the connection is trusted. I wanted to see this from the inside. So I created my own Root CA, used it to sign a certificate for a test site called mytestsite.local , and made both Chrome and curl trust it. My setup: a Windows laptop, the server running in WSL2 (Ubuntu 20.04, OpenSSL 1.1.1f), and Chrome on Windows. Tip on the hostname: I used mytestsite.local , and it worked fine on my machine. If you repeat this, consider mytestsite.test instead. .local is reserved for multicast DNS (mDNS) and can cause name-resolution conflicts on some networks, while .test is reserved for testing ( RFC 6761 ). summary: How incident response differs on AWS Incident response on AWS is faster to execute and easier to get wrong than on-premises response, because both the attacker and the responder work through the same APIs. Containment is an API call. So is destroying evidence. Four differences drive the rest of this article: Shared responsibility sets your scope. AWS secures the infrastructure. You respond to what happens with your identities, configurations, data and workloads. Identity comes first. Most AWS incidents begin with valid credentials. Containing a principal usually matters more than containing a host. Resources are short-lived. An instance in an Auto Scaling group or a Fargate task can disappear before you look at it. Evidence capture has to be prepared in advance and quick. Everything can be automated. Any step you can run from the CLI can run from a Lambda function or a Systems Manager runbook, with the same permissions problem if you grant too much. Two references frame the lifecycle. NIST SP 800-61 Revision 3, published in April 2025, replaced Revision 2 and maps incident response onto the six functions of the Cybersecurity Framework 2.0 (NIST). The AWS Security Incident Response Guide organises the work as preparation, operations and post-incident activity (AWS technical guide). This article uses the operational phases responders actually work through: Preparation Detection and analysis Containment Forensic acquisition Eradication and recovery Post-incident activity Command

summary: Introduction: Why SSH Configuration Drift Is a Real Security Risk Security in cloud environments is not a one-time setup. It is a continuous process. One of the most overlooked but dangerous problems in managing a fleet of EC2 instances is configuration drift — the gradual deviation of a system's actual state from its desired, secure baseline. SSH (Secure Shell) is the primary remote access protocol for Linux-based EC2 instances. The /etc/ssh/sshd_config file controls how the SSH daemon behaves on a server. A single misconfigured directive in this file can open the door to serious security vulnerabilities. For example, PermitRootLogin yes allows direct root access over SSH, which means an attacker who obtains valid credentials — or exploits a brute-force vulnerability — can gain full administrative control of the server without any additional privilege escalation. This is not a theoretical risk. CIS (Center for Internet Security) Benchmarks, PCI-DSS, HIPAA, and SOC 2 compliance frameworks all explicitly require that root login over SSH be disabled. Failing this check during an audit can result in compliance violations, financial penalties, and reputational damage. The challenge is that in a dynamic cloud environment, configuration drift happens constantly. A developer might temporarily enable root login to debug an issue and forget to revert it. summary: Hello Everyone 👋 Picture a pull request with a tiny diff. Someone tidies the support bot's system prompt. Three lines go away because the prompt "felt long" and tokens cost money. I built a small regression gate for prompts , then tried to break it with real models: Llama 3.2 3B (Meta), Qwen 2.5 1.5B (Alibaba) and Gemma 3 1B (Google), all running on my own RTX 4060 through Ollama. Six versions of one prompt, sixteen test cases, 1,710 recorded answers , and an AWS bill of $0, which is how I like my experiments. Here is the teaser. One "tidy" edit moved the overall score from 84.2% to 80.0%, which looks like noise. Underneath, a refund rule had collapsed from 10 of 10 correct answers to 3 of 10. The gate blocked it. The same experiment also blocked a fix that was genuinely good, passed an edit I was sure would fail, and showed me that "temperature 0" is more of a suggestion than a promise. This article walks through the experiment the way I lived it: the setup, the five rules, what went wrong with my own graders, and what the numbers actually say (and do not say). TL;DR A prompt change can leave the overall score flat while breaking one important behaviour. The gate caught that with per-case rules, not with the overall number. On Llama 3.2 3B, two of four prompt changes were blocked and two passed.
